"'''You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin''''{{-"}} is a song by [[Phil Spector]], [[Barry Mann]], and [[Cynthia Weil]], first recorded in 1964 by the American vocal duo [[the Righteous Brothers]] and released as the lone single and title track from their 1965 album of the same name. This version, produced by Spector, is cited by some music critics as the ultimate expression and illustration of his [[Wall of Sound]] recording technique.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/entertainment/3246887.stm |title=Brothers in good company with hits|last= Dowling |first= Stephen |publisher=BBC }}</ref> The record was a critical and commercial success on its release, reaching number one in early February 1965 in both the United States and the United Kingdom. The single ranked No. 5 in [[Billboard (magazine)|''Billboard'']]'s [[Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1965|year-end Top 100 of 1965]] [[Billboard Hot 100|Hot 100]] hits – based on combined airplay and sales, and not including three charted weeks in December 1964 – and has entered the UK Top Ten on three occasions.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.songfacts.com/detail.php?id=429 |title=You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin' |work=Song Facts |access-date=November 16, 2015 |archive-date=November 26, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071126080952/http://www.songfacts.com/detail.php?id=429 |url-status=live }}</ref>

"You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin{{' "}} has been covered successfully by numerous artists. In 1965, [[Cilla Black]]'s recording reached No. 2 in the [[UK Singles Chart]]. [[Dionne Warwick]] took her version to No. 16 on the ''Billboard'' Hot 100 chart in 1969. A 1971 duet version by singers [[Roberta Flack]] and [[Donny Hathaway]] peaked at No. 30 on the ''Billboard'' R&B singles chart. [[Long John Baldry]] charted at No. 2 in Australia with his 1979 remake and a 1980 version by [[Hall and Oates]] reached No. 12 on the US Hot 100.

Various music writers have described the Righteous Brothers version as "one of the best records ever made" and "the ultimate pop record".<ref name="sullivan"/> In 1999 the performing-rights organization Broadcast Music, Inc. (BMI) ranked the song as the most-played song on American radio and television in the 20th century, having accumulated more than 8 million airplays by 1999,<ref name="BMI">{{cite web |url=http://www.bmi.com/news/entry/232893 |title=News | BMI Announces Top 100 Songs of the Century |publisher=BMI.com |date=December 13, 1999 |access-date=March 28, 2013 |archive-date=June 16, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120616030322/http://www.bmi.com/news/entry/232893 |url-status=live }}</ref> and nearly 15 million by 2011.<ref name="brown eye girl"/> It held the distinction of being the most-played song for 22 years until 2019, when it was overtaken by "[[Every Breath You Take]]".<ref name="BMI 2019"/> In 2001 the song was chosen as one of the [[Songs of the Century]] by [[RIAA]], and in 2003 the track ranked No. 34 on the list of the [[500 Greatest Songs of All Time]] by ''[[Rolling Stone]]''. In 2015, the single was inducted into the [[National Recording Registry]] by the [[Library of Congress]] for being "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant".<ref name="loc">{{cite web |url=https://www.loc.gov/today/pr/2015/15-041.html |title=New Entries to National Recording Registry | News Releases - Library of Congress |publisher=Loc.gov |access-date=October 13, 2015 |archive-date=March 4, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304081256/http://www.acclaimedmusic.net/Current/Radiohead.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> {{toclimit|3}}

In 1964, music producer [[Phil Spector]] conducted the band at a show in San Francisco where the Righteous Brothers was also appearing, and he was impressed enough with the duo to want them to record for his own label, [[Philles Records]].<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-gwHkKmuqDwC&pg=PA201 |title=The 100 Greatest Rock 'n' Roll Songs Ever |last=Mednick |first=Avram |page=201 |publisher=iUniverse |date=June 12, 2000 |isbn=978-0595093045 |access-date=November 9, 2015 |archive-date=May 20, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160520122654/https://books.google.com/books?id=-gwHkKmuqDwC&pg=PA201 |url-status=live }}</ref> All the songs previously produced by Spector for Philles Records featured African-American singers, and the Righteous Brothers would be his first white vocal act. However, they had a vocal style, termed [[blue-eyed soul]], that suited Spector.<ref name="google1">{{cite book |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=vyyVGNycEA0C&pg=PT117 |page=PT117 |title=Phil Spector: Out Of His Head|last= Williams |first= Richard |publisher= Omnibus Press |edition= Revised |date=November 17, 2009 |isbn=9780857120564}}</ref>

When Spector joined in with the writing, he added "gone, gone, gone, whoa, whoa, whoa" to the end of the chorus, which Weil disliked.<ref name="wsj">{{cite web |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052702303343404577519042622092010 |title=The Song That Conquered Radio |work=The Wall Street Journal |last=Myers |first=Marc |date=July 12, 2012 |access-date=March 12, 2017 |archive-date=November 13, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171113113625/https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052702303343404577519042622092010 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |url= http://www.newyorker.com/culture/culture-desk/mann-and-weil-on-broadway |title= Mann and Weil on Broadway |last= Larson |first= Sarah |date= November 26, 2013 |magazine= The New Yorker |access-date= November 10, 2015 |archive-date= November 25, 2015 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20151125131817/http://www.newyorker.com/culture/culture-desk/mann-and-weil-on-broadway |url-status= live }}</ref> The line "you've lost that lovin' feelin{{' "}} was originally only intended to be a dummy line that would be replaced later, but Spector liked it and decided to keep it.<ref name="sullivan"/> The form of the song is of verse-chorus-verse-chorus-bridge-chorus or ABABCB form.<ref>Friedman, Sidney (2007). "In the Middle of the Music" lecture notes</ref> Mann and Weil had problems writing the bridge and the ending, and asked Spector for help. Spector experimented on the piano with a "[[Hang On Sloopy]]" riff that they then built on for the bridge.<ref name="wsj"/>

[[Bill Medley]], who has the low voice, seemed to like the song."<ref name="Hinckley, David 1991"/> However, Medley initially felt that the song did not suit their more uptempo [[rhythm and blues]] style, and Mann and Spector had sung the song in a higher key: "And we just thought, 'Wow, what a good song for [[The Everly Brothers]].' But it didn't seem right for us."<ref name="songfacts">{{cite web |url=http://www.songfacts.com/blog/interviews/bill_medley_of_the_righteous_brothers/ |title=Bill Medley of The later Righteous Brothers |work=Songfacts |access-date=November 11, 2015 |archive-date=October 18, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151018130338/http://www.songfacts.com/blog/interviews/bill_medley_of_the_righteous_brothers/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="pophistory"/> The song, which has a very big [[Range (music)|range]], was originally written in the higher key of F. When Hatfield asked Spector just what he was supposed to do during Medley's solo, Spector replied, "You can go directly to the bank!"<ref name="Hinckley, David 1991">{{cite web |url=http://albumlinernotes.com/Back_To_Mono__Songs_.html |author=Hinckley, David |year=1991 |title=Back To Mono (Songs) |access-date=November 24, 2015 |archive-date=November 24, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151124210606/http://albumlinernotes.com/Back_To_Mono__Songs_.html |url-status=live }} Notes from ''Phil Spector: Back to Mono (1958-1969)'' boxed-set booklet, see the recording details for the song</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/lists/500-greatest-albums-of-all-time-20120531/phil-spector-back-to-mono-1958-1969-20120524 |title=500 Greatest Albums of All Time : 65 - Phil Spector, 'Back to Mono (1958-1969)' |magazine=Rolling Stone |date=May 31, 2009 |access-date=September 19, 2017 |archive-date=September 19, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170919191319/http://www.rollingstone.com/music/lists/500-greatest-albums-of-all-time-20120531/phil-spector-back-to-mono-1958-1969-20120524 |url-status=live }}</ref>

thumb|upright|Phil Spector in 1965
In 1964, music producer Phil Spector conducted the band at a show in San Francisco where the Righteous Brothers was also appearing, and he was impressed enough with the duo to want them to record for his own label, Philles Records. All the songs previously produced by Spector for Philles Records featured African-American singers, and the Righteous Brothers would be his first white vocal act. However, they had a vocal style, termed blue-eyed soul, that suited Spector.

Spector commissioned Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil to write a song for them, bringing them over from New York to Los Angeles to stay at the Chateau Marmont so they could write the song. Taking a cue from "Baby I Need Your Loving" by The Four Tops, which was then rising in the charts, Mann and Weil decided to write a ballad. Mann wrote the melody first, and came up with the opening line, "You never close your eyes anymore when I kiss your lips", influenced by a line from the song "I Love How You Love Me" that was co-written by Mann and produced by Spector – "I love how your eyes close whenever you kiss me". Mann and Weil wrote the first two verses quickly, including the chorus line "you've lost that lovin' feelin{{' "}}. When Spector joined in with the writing, he added "gone, gone, gone, whoa, whoa, whoa" to the end of the chorus, which Weil disliked. The line "you've lost that lovin' feelin{{' "}} was originally only intended to be a dummy line that would be replaced later, but Spector liked it and decided to keep it. The form of the song is of verse-chorus-verse-chorus-bridge-chorus or ABABCB form. Mann and Weil had problems writing the bridge and the ending, and asked Spector for help. Spector experimented on the piano with a "Hang On Sloopy" riff that they then built on for the bridge.

Weil recalled that, "after Phil, Barry and I finished [writing it], we took it over to the Righteous Brothers. Bill Medley, who has the low voice, seemed to like the song." However, Medley initially felt that the song did not suit their more uptempo rhythm and blues style, and Mann and Spector had sung the song in a higher key: "And we just thought, 'Wow, what a good song for The Everly Brothers.' But it didn't seem right for us." The song, which has a very big range, was originally written in the higher key of F. But to accommodate Medley's baritone voice, the key was gradually lowered to C{{music|sharp}} in the recording, which, together with slowing the song down, changed the "whole vibe of the song", according to Medley.

Bobby Hatfield reportedly expressed his annoyance to Spector when he learned that Medley would start the first verse alone and that he had to wait until the chorus before joining in. Prior to this, they would have been given equal prominence in a song. When Hatfield asked Spector just what he was supposed to do during Medley's solo, Spector replied, "You can go directly to the bank!"

sections.heading: The Righteous Brothers recording
sections.wikitext:
[[File:TheRighteousBrothersperformingKBF.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|The Righteous Brothers performing at [[Knott's Berry Farm]] in the 1970s]]
The song was recorded on September 26, 1964, at Studio A of [[Gold Star Studios]] in Los Angeles.<ref name=mix /><ref name="sullivan"/> When Hatfield and Medley went to record the vocals a few weeks after the song was written, all the instrumental tracks had already been recorded and overdubbed.<ref name="wsj"/> They recorded the vocal many times – Medley sang the opening verse over and over again until Spector was satisfied, and the process was then repeated with the next verse. The recording took over 39 takes and around eight hours over a period of two days.<ref name="sullivan"/><ref name="wsj"/>

The song would become one of the foremost examples of Spector's "[[Wall of Sound]]" technique. It features the studio musicians [[The Wrecking Crew (music)|the Wrecking Crew]]; playing on this recording were [[Don Randi]] on piano, [[Tommy Tedesco]] on guitar, [[Carol Kaye]] and [[Ray Pohlman]] on bass, and [[Steve Douglas (saxophonist)|Steve Douglas]] on sax.<ref name="randi"/> They were also joined by [[Barney Kessel]] on guitar and [[Earl Palmer]] on drums. [[Jack Nitzsche]] usually arranged the songs for Spector, but he was absent, and the arrangement was done by [[Gene Page]].<ref name="google1"/><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/obituary-gene-page-1199645.html |title=Obituary: Gene Page |last=Perrone |first=Pierre |date=October 23, 2011 |work=The Independent |access-date=September 19, 2017 |archive-date=April 8, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190408155834/https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/obituary-gene-page-1199645.html |url-status=live }}</ref> As with his other songs, Spector started by cutting the instrumental track first, building up layers of sound to create the Wall of Sound effect. The recording was done mono so Spector could fix the sound exactly as he wanted it.<ref name=mix /> According to sound engineer [[Larry Levine]], they started recording four acoustic guitars; when that was ready, they added the pianos, of which there were three; followed by three basses; the horns (two trumpets, two trombones, and three saxophones); then finally the drums.<ref name=mix>{{cite web |url=https://www.mixonline.com/recording/classic-tracks/classic-tracks-righteous-brothers-youve-lost-lovin-feeling-365140 |title=Classic Tracks: The Righteous Brothers' "You've Lost That Lovin' Feeling" |date=March 1, 2002 |last=Daley |first=Dan |work=Mix |access-date=November 10, 2015 |archive-date=November 17, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117031850/http://www.mixonline.com/news/profiles/classic-tracks-righteous-brothers-youve-lost-lovin-feeling/365140 |url-status=live }}</ref> The vocals by Hatfield and Medley were then recorded and the strings overdubbed.<ref name="sullivan"/> The background singers were mainly the vocal group [[the Blossoms]], accompanied by [[the Ronettes]]<ref>{{cite book |last1=Musso |first1=Anthony P. |title=Setting the Record Straight: The Music and Careers of Recording Artists from the 1950s and Early 1960s in Their Own Words |date=207 |publisher=AuthorHouse |location=Bloomington, IN; Milton Keynes, UK |isbn=978-1425959869 |page=293 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JiBKaCWt9_IC&pg=PA293 |access-date=26 July 2024}}</ref> and joined in the song's crescendo by a young and then-unknown [[Cher]].<ref>{{cite book |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=AEnWG6qjckIC&pg=PA165 |title= The Last Sultan: The Life and Times of Ahmet Ertegun |last= Greenfield |first= Robert |page= 165 |publisher= Simon & Schuster; Reprint edition |date= November 6, 2012 |isbn= 978-1416558408 |access-date= November 28, 2015 |archive-date= April 25, 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160425150455/https://books.google.com/books?id=AEnWG6qjckIC&pg=PA165 |url-status= live }}</ref> [[Reverb]] was applied in the recording, and more was added on the lead vocals during the mix.<ref name=mix /> According to music writer [[Robert Palmer (American writer)|Robert Palmer]], the effect of the technique used was to create a sound that was "deliberately blurry, atmospheric, and of course huge; Wagnerian rock 'n' roll with all the trimmings."<ref name="sullivan"/>

The song was recorded on September 26, 1964, at Studio A of Gold Star Studios in Los Angeles. When Hatfield and Medley went to record the vocals a few weeks after the song was written, all the instrumental tracks had already been recorded and overdubbed. They recorded the vocal many times – Medley sang the opening verse over and over again until Spector was satisfied, and the process was then repeated with the next verse. The recording took over 39 takes and around eight hours over a period of two days.

The song would become one of the foremost examples of Spector's "Wall of Sound" technique. It features the studio musicians the Wrecking Crew; playing on this recording were Don Randi on piano, Tommy Tedesco on guitar, Carol Kaye and Ray Pohlman on bass, and Steve Douglas on sax. They were also joined by Barney Kessel on guitar and Earl Palmer on drums. Jack Nitzsche usually arranged the songs for Spector, but he was absent, and the arrangement was done by Gene Page. As with his other songs, Spector started by cutting the instrumental track first, building up layers of sound to create the Wall of Sound effect. The recording was done mono so Spector could fix the sound exactly as he wanted it. According to sound engineer Larry Levine, they started recording four acoustic guitars; when that was ready, they added the pianos, of which there were three; followed by three basses; the horns (two trumpets, two trombones, and three saxophones); then finally the drums. The vocals by Hatfield and Medley were then recorded and the strings overdubbed. The background singers were mainly the vocal group the Blossoms, accompanied by the Ronettes and joined in the song's crescendo by a young and then-unknown Cher. Reverb was applied in the recording, and more was added on the lead vocals during the mix. According to music writer Robert Palmer, the effect of the technique used was to create a sound that was "deliberately blurry, atmospheric, and of course huge; Wagnerian rock 'n' roll with all the trimmings."

The recorded song was three ticks slower and a tone and a half lower than what Mann and Weil had written. When Mann heard the finished record over the phone, he thought that it had been mistakenly played at 33 1/3 instead of 45 rpm and told Spector, "Phil, you have it on the wrong speed!"

Even with his interest in the song, Medley had his doubts because it was unusually long for a pop song at the time. In an interview with Rolling Stone magazine, he recalled, "We had no idea if it would be a hit. It was too slow, too long, and right in the middle of The Beatles and the British Invasion." The song ran for nearly four minutes when released. This was too long by contemporary AM radio standards; radio stations at that time rarely played songs longer than three minutes because longer songs meant that fewer ads could be placed between song sets. Spector, however, refused to shorten it. Following a suggestion by Larry Levine, Spector had "3:05" printed on the label, instead of the track's actual running time of 3:45. He also added a false ending which made the recording more dramatic, and also tricked radio DJs into thinking it was a shorter song.

Spector took these as criticisms and later said: "I didn't sleep for a week when that record came out. I was so sick, I got a spastic colon; I had an ulcer."

In 1998, the original 1964 recording of the song on the Philles label was inducted into the [[Grammy Hall of Fame]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.grammy.com/awards/hall-of-fame-award#y|title=GRAMMY Hall Of Fame | Hall of Fame Artists | GRAMMY.com|website=grammy.com}}</ref>

In 2001, this recording was ranked at No. 9 in the list of [[Songs of the Century]] released by the [[Recording Industry Association of America]] and the [[National Endowment for the Arts]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2001/SHOWBIZ/Music/03/08/365.folo/ |title=Songs of the Century' list: The debate goes on |date=March 8, 2001 |last=Allen |first=Jamie |work=CNN |access-date=December 18, 2015 |archive-date=March 5, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305020849/http://edition.cnn.com/2001/SHOWBIZ/Music/03/08/365.folo/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2004, the same recording was ranked at No. 34 by ''[[Rolling Stone]]'' magazine in their list of the [[Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs of All Time|500 Greatest Songs of All Time]].<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/lists/the-500-greatest-songs-of-all-time-20110407/smokey-robinson-and-the-miracles-the-tracks-of-my-tears-20110526 |title=500 Greatest Songs of All Time |magazine=Rolling Stone |date=December 11, 2003 |access-date=September 19, 2017 |archive-date=September 21, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170921183525/http://www.rollingstone.com/music/lists/the-500-greatest-songs-of-all-time-20110407/smokey-robinson-and-the-miracles-the-tracks-of-my-tears-20110526 |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2005, "You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin{{' "}} was awarded the [[Songwriters Hall of Fame]]'s Towering Song Award presented to "the creators of an individual song that has influenced the culture in a unique way over many years".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.songwritershalloffame.org/ceremony/entry/C3126/5148 |title=2005 Award & Induction Ceremony |work=Songwriter Hall of Fame |access-date=December 16, 2015 |archive-date=December 22, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151222090513/http://www.songwritershalloffame.org/ceremony/entry/C3126/5148 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2015, the [[National Recording Registry]] of the [[Library of Congress]], which each year selects from 130 years of sound recordings for special recognition and preservation, chose the Righteous Brothers rendition as one of the 25 recordings that have "cultural, artistic and/or historical significance to American society and the nation's audio legacy".<ref name="loc"/><ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.latimes.com/entertainment/music/posts/la-et-ms-library-congress-doors-righteous-brothers-national-recording-registry-20150323-story.html |title=Library of Congress welcomes recordings by the Doors, Righteous Brothers |work=The Los Angeles Times |last=Lewis |first=Randy |date=March 25, 2015 |access-date=December 16, 2015 |archive-date=December 22, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151222082446/http://www.latimes.com/entertainment/music/posts/la-et-ms-library-congress-doors-righteous-brothers-national-recording-registry-20150323-story.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

sections.heading: Background
sections.wikitext: British singer [[Cilla Black]] first achieved major chart success by covering [[Dionne Warwick]]'s newly released American hit "[[Anyone Who Had a Heart (song)|Anyone Who Had a Heart]]" for the UK market, which gave her a number-one hit in both the [[UK Singles Chart]] and the [[Irish Singles Chart]] in February 1964, out-performing Warwick's original version, which only peaked at No. 42 in the UK. Black's producer [[George Martin]] repeated this strategy with the Righteous Brothers "You've Lost That Lovin' Feeling" that had just been released in the US. Black's version is shorter with an abbreviated bridge, of which she said: "I don't want people to get bored".<ref>{{cite book| first=Richard| last=Williams| date=November 17, 2009| title=Phil Spector: out of his head| publisher=Omnibus Press| location=London| page=PT100| edition= Revised| isbn=9780857120564| url= https://books.google.com/books?id=vyyVGNycEA0C&pg=PT100| access-date=December 16, 2015}}</ref> The abridgement also removed the necessity of Black's attempting to match the Righteous Brothers' climactic vocal trade-off.
sections.text: British singer Cilla Black first achieved major chart success by covering Dionne Warwick's newly released American hit "Anyone Who Had a Heart" for the UK market, which gave her a number-one hit in both the UK Singles Chart and the Irish Singles Chart in February 1964, out-performing Warwick's original version, which only peaked at No. 42 in the UK. Black's producer George Martin repeated this strategy with the Righteous Brothers "You've Lost That Lovin' Feeling" that had just been released in the US. Black's version is shorter with an abbreviated bridge, of which she said: "I don't want people to get bored". The abridgement also removed the necessity of Black's attempting to match the Righteous Brothers' climactic vocal trade-off.

sections.heading: Chart rivalry
sections.wikitext:
Both Black's and the Righteous Brothers versions of the song debuted on the UK chart in the same week in January 1965, with Black debuting higher at No. 28.<ref name="uk chart2">{{cite web |url= http://www.officialcharts.com/search/singles/you%27ve%20lost%20that%20lovin%27%20feelin%27/ |title= You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin' |work= Official UK Charts Company |access-date= November 8, 2015 |archive-date= October 23, 2015 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20151023114327/http://www.officialcharts.com/search/singles/you%27ve%20lost%20that%20lovin%27%20feelin%27/ |url-status= live }} Click on Chart Facts for complete charting information</ref> According to [[Tony Hall (music executive)|Tony Hall]] of [[Decca Records]] who was responsible for promoting the Righteous Brothers record in the UK, Black's version was preferred by BBC radio where one of its DJs{{who|date=June 2023}} disparaged the Righteous Brothers' version as a "dirge" and refused to play it. Hall therefore requested that Spector send the Righteous Brothers over to Britain to promote the song so it might have a chance on the chart.<ref name="independent">{{cite news|url= https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/bobby-hatfield-37420.html|title= Obituaries: Bobby Hatfield|work= The Independent|last= Leigh|first= Spencer|date= November 7, 2003|access-date= September 19, 2017|archive-date= June 23, 2018|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180623020432/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/bobby-hatfield-37420.html|url-status= live}}</ref><ref name="brown"/>

The following week Black remained in ascendancy at No. 12 with the Righteous Brothers at No. 20. The Righteous Brothers came over to Britain, spent a week promoting the song and performed for television shows in Manchester and Birmingham.<ref name="independent"/> At the same time, Andrew Loog Oldham placed a full-page ad in ''Melody Maker'' promoting the Righteous Brothers version at his own initiative and expense, and urged the readers to watch the Righteous Brothers appearance on the ITV television show ''[[Ready Steady Go!]]''<ref name="brown"/> In its third week on the February 3, 1965, chart, Black jumped to No. 2, while the Righteous Brothers made an even larger jump to No. 3. Hall recalled meeting at a party [[Brian Epstein]], the manager of Black, who said that Black's version would be number one and told Hall, "You haven't a hope in hell."<ref name="brown"/>

However, in its fourth week, Black's version began its descent, dropping to No. 5, while the Righteous Brothers climbed to number one.<ref name="uk chart2" /> Cilla Black then reportedly cabled her congratulations to the Righteous Brothers on their reaching number one.<ref name="brown"/> Black's version of "You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin{{' "}} would prove to be her highest charting UK single apart from her two number ones: "[[Anyone Who Had a Heart (song)|Anyone Who Had a Heart]]" and "[[You're My World]]". While Black's version was released in Ireland, it did not make the official Irish Singles Chart as published by [[RTÉ]], but it reached No. 5 on the unofficial ''[[The Herald (Ireland)|Evening Herald]]'' charts.{{Citation needed|date=September 2018}}

Black remade "You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin{{' "}} for her 1985 ''[[Surprisingly Cilla]]'' album.
sections.text:
Both Black's and the Righteous Brothers versions of the song debuted on the UK chart in the same week in January 1965, with Black debuting higher at No. 28. According to Tony Hall of Decca Records who was responsible for promoting the Righteous Brothers record in the UK, Black's version was preferred by BBC radio where one of its DJs{{who|date=June 2023}} disparaged the Righteous Brothers' version as a "dirge" and refused to play it. Hall therefore requested that Spector send the Righteous Brothers over to Britain to promote the song so it might have a chance on the chart.

The following week Black remained in ascendancy at No. 12 with the Righteous Brothers at No. 20. The Righteous Brothers came over to Britain, spent a week promoting the song and performed for television shows in Manchester and Birmingham. At the same time, Andrew Loog Oldham placed a full-page ad in Melody Maker promoting the Righteous Brothers version at his own initiative and expense, and urged the readers to watch the Righteous Brothers appearance on the ITV television show Ready Steady Go! In its third week on the February 3, 1965, chart, Black jumped to No. 2, while the Righteous Brothers made an even larger jump to No. 3. Hall recalled meeting at a party Brian Epstein, the manager of Black, who said that Black's version would be number one and told Hall, "You haven't a hope in hell."

However, in its fourth week, Black's version began its descent, dropping to No. 5, while the Righteous Brothers climbed to number one. Cilla Black then reportedly cabled her congratulations to the Righteous Brothers on their reaching number one. Black's version of "You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin{{' "}} would prove to be her highest charting UK single apart from her two number ones: "Anyone Who Had a Heart" and "You're My World". While Black's version was released in Ireland, it did not make the official Irish Singles Chart as published by RTÉ, but it reached No. 5 on the unofficial Evening Herald charts.{{Citation needed|date=September 2018}}

Black remade "You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin{{' "}} for her 1985 Surprisingly Cilla album.

sections.wikitext: In 1969, American singer [[Dionne Warwick]] recorded a cover version of "You've Lost That Lovin' Feeling" for her studio album ''[[Soulful (Dionne Warwick album)|Soulful]]''. Her version was the only single released from the album and it was aimed to showcase Warwick as more of an R&B singer than was evidenced by her work with [[Burt Bacharach]]. Co-produced by Warwick and [[Chips Moman]] and recorded at American Sound Studios in [[Memphis, Tennessee]], ''Soulful'' was one of Warwick's most successful albums peaking at No. 11 on the [[Billboard 200]] album chart. The single "You've Lost That Lovin' Feeling" reached No. 16 on the ''Billboard'' Hot 100 chart, and charted at No. 13 on the ''Billboard'' R&B singles chart.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/onthisdayinblack00warn |url-access=registration |title=On this Day in Black Music History|last= Warner |first= Jay | publisher= Hal Leonard Corporation |page=[https://archive.org/details/onthisdayinblack00warn/page/279 279]|date=April 26, 2006|isbn=978-0634099267}}</ref> In Australia the ''[[Go-Set]]'' Top 40 chart ranked Warwick's version of "You've Lost That Lovin' Feeling" with a No. 34 peak in January 1970.<ref name="go set aus">{{cite web |url=http://www.poparchives.com.au/gosetcharts/1970/19700110.html |title=10 January 1970: Singles |work=Go-Set Charts |access-date=April 8, 2016 |archive-date=August 29, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160829074357/http://www.poparchives.com.au/gosetcharts/1970/19700110.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> In Warwick's version of the song, she spells the last word of the title out fully as "feeling" rather than the usual "feelin{{' "}}.
sections.text: In 1969, American singer Dionne Warwick recorded a cover version of "You've Lost That Lovin' Feeling" for her studio album Soulful. Her version was the only single released from the album and it was aimed to showcase Warwick as more of an R&B singer than was evidenced by her work with Burt Bacharach. Co-produced by Warwick and Chips Moman and recorded at American Sound Studios in Memphis, Tennessee, Soulful was one of Warwick's most successful albums peaking at No. 11 on the Billboard 200 album chart. The single "You've Lost That Lovin' Feeling" reached No. 16 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart, and charted at No. 13 on the Billboard R&B singles chart. In Australia the Go-Set Top 40 chart ranked Warwick's version of "You've Lost That Lovin' Feeling" with a No. 34 peak in January 1970. sections.wikitext: In 1971, American singers [[Roberta Flack]] and [[Donny Hathaway]] recorded a cover version of "You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin{{' "}}. sections.wikitext:
In 1979, British-Canadian [[blues]] singer [[Long John Baldry]] recorded a cover version of "You've Lost That Loving Feeling{{' "}} as a duet with American singer [[Kathi McDonald]] for his album ''Baldry's Out'', the Jimmy Horowitz-produced disc which was Baldry's first recording in his newly adopted homeland of [[Canada]].<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.noise11.com/news/kathi-mcdonald-dead-at-64-20121005 |title= Kathi McDonald Dead At 64 |last= Cashmere |first= Paul |date= October 5, 2012 |work= Noise11 |access-date= November 16, 2015 |archive-date= June 17, 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180617115556/http://www.noise11.com/news/kathi-mcdonald-dead-at-64-20121005 |url-status= live }}</ref> In this version, Kathi McDonald sang the latter half of the first verse using the part from the second verse ("It makes me just feel like crying ..."), inverting the usual order.

Released as a single that summer, Baldry's "You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin{{' "}} charted at No. 45 on the Canadian ''[[RPM (magazine)|RPM]]'' singles chart, and spilled over into the US ''Billboard'' Hot 100 chart at No. 89. The single also reached No. 2 in Australia in 1980.<ref name="baldry aus">{{cite book|last=Kent|first=David|author-link=David Kent (historian)|title=Australian Chart Book 1970–1992|publisher=Australian Chart Book|location=St. Ives, N.S.W.|year=1993|edition=Illustrated|page=25|isbn=0-646-11917-6}}</ref> Bill Medley of the Righteous Brothers told Baldry that he liked their remake of the song better than his own.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/itainteasylongjo0098myer |url-access=registration |title=It Ain't Easy: Long John Baldry and the Birth of the British Blues|last=Myers |first=Paul |page=[https://archive.org/details/itainteasylongjo0098myer/page/194 194] |publisher=Greystone Books, Canada |date=September 30, 2007|isbn= 978-1553652007 }}</ref> Baldry had first recorded the song – as "You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin{{' "}} – for his 1966 album ''Looking at Long John''. The Baldry/McDonald duet version of "You've Lost That Loving Feeling" also reached No. 37 in New Zealand.

The song is highly popular on the radio; according to the performing-rights organization Broadcast Music, Inc. (BMI), it became the most-played song of all time on American radio in 1997 with over 7 million airplays (all versions), overtaking the Beatles' "Yesterday". At the end of 1999, the song was ranked by the BMI as the most-played song of the 20th century, having been broadcast more than 8 million times on American radio and television, and it remains the most-played song, having accumulated almost 15 million airplays in the US by 2011. The song also received 11 BMI Pop Awards by 1997, the most for any song, and has received 14 in total so far. In 2019, "Every Breath You Take" by The Police displaced it as the most played song on US radio.

The popularity of the song also means that it is one of the highest grossing songs for its copyright holders. It was estimated by the BBC programme The Richest Songs in the World in 2012 to be the third biggest earner of royalties of all songs, behind "White Christmas" and "Happy Birthday to You".
